methods.label: Expose a nonpositive square
methods.explanation:
The two logarithm bases suggest using change of base to express everything in one positive quantity. All logarithms are defined because \(a\ge b>1\). Set
\[
t=\log_b a\ge1.
\]
Change of base gives \(\log_a b=1/t\). Using the quotient rule for logarithms, the expression becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log_a\left(\frac ab\right)
+\log_b\left(\frac ba\right)
&=2-\frac1t-t\\
&=-\frac{(t-1)^2}{t}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The numerator is a square and the denominator is positive, so this is at most zero. Equality holds exactly when \(t=1\), meaning \(a=b\). Such pairs are allowed, for example \(a=b=2\). Therefore the largest value is \(\boxed{0}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: Logarithm laws, change of base, and a nonnegative-square argument are standard precalculus reasoning.

methods.label: Bound two positive reciprocal quantities
methods.explanation:
Let \(u=\log_a b\) and \(v=\log_b a\). Both are positive because \(a,b>1\), and change of base shows
\[
uv=\frac{\log b}{\log a}
\frac{\log a}{\log b}=1.
\]
The quotient rule rewrites the requested expression as
\[
\log_a\left(\frac ab\right)
+\log_b\left(\frac ba\right)=2-u-v.
\]
For the positive numbers \(u\) and \(v\), AM-GM gives
\[
u+v\ge2\sqrt{uv}=2.
\]
Thus the expression is at most zero. Equality requires \(u=v\); together with \(uv=1\) and positivity, this gives \(u=v=1\), or \(a=b\). Taking \(a=b=2\) attains equality, so the largest value is \(\boxed{0}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: The two-variable AM-GM inequality, including its positivity and equality conditions, is an accessible high-school alternative.
